Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 359 Aerial Ungulate Survey - 2015 
 
Background 
Winters from 2000 to 2006 were unusually mild, allowing for rapid growth of ungulate populations. To address 
concerns of agricultural depredation by deer, hunting opportunities were increase for both species. Following 
several recent winters with deep snow and colder temperatures and perceived declines in both mule and white -
tailed deer, there has been increasing public concern over the populations of mule deer and white -tailed deer in 
WMU 359.  
 
Moose populations in WMU 359 declined abruptly following a winter tick outbreak in 2006 -07, and numbers have 
been slow to recover. The objectives of this survey were to assess the status of moose and mule deer since the 
last survey in 2008, determine a population estimate, population ratios for sex and age classes, and a density 
estimate for moose and mule deer within Wildlife Management Unit 359.  
 
Survey method 
Distance sampling methods were used to determine population estimates for moose and deer, as described in the 
Distance Sampling Chapter of the Aerial Ungulate Survey Protocol Manual (ESRD, 2014). Sampling transects 
were oriented north-south, 10km long, 1.6 km apart with a gap of 1.2 km between the endpoints of the transects. 
Although elk were observed on this survey, loss of snow cover at the end of the survey prevented us from 
achieving a reliable minimum total count for WMU 359.    
 
Results 
From February 17 to 26, 2015, we flew 201 transects for a total survey effort of 1041 km and 33.4 hrs flying time. 
In total, 369 moose were observed from 237 independent groups of moose. Of the 359 moose that were 
successfully classified, 58 (16%) were bulls, 219 (61%) were cows, and 82 (23%) were calves. Of the 58 bulls 
observed, 56 had already shed their antlers, while two small bulls were observed with antlers. The bull:cow and 
calf:cow ratio were 0.37 and 0.26, respectively. The final density estimate was 0.619 moose/km2 with a log -based 
90% confidence interval from 0.518 to 0.739 moose/km 2 and a CV of 10.8%. The estimated moose abundance for 
WMU 359 is 2047 (90% CI 1714, 2446). 
 
In total, 418 mule deer were observed from 67 independent groups of mule deer. Of the 354 mule deer classified 
there were 33 bucks (9%), 253 does (71%) and 68 fawns (19%). The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratio were 0 .13 and 
0.27, respectively. The final density estimate was 0.668 mule deer/km 2 with a log-based 90% confidence interval 
from 0.445 to 1.002 and a CV of 24.9%. The estimated mule deer abundance for WMU 359 is 2209 (90% CI 
1472, 3317).

In total, 258 individuals were observed from 26 groups of white-tailed deer. Of the 142 white-tailed deer classified, 
7 were bucks (5%), 94 were does (66%) and 41 were fawns (29%). The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratio were 0.07 
and 0.44, respectively. The number of groups observed was insufficient for a density estimate. 
A total of 595 elk were observed from 45 groups with a bull:cow and calf:cow ratio of 0.52 and 0.31, respectively. 
Note that this is not a complete minimum total count of elk in this WMU.
